v_incentive_register.conditions: Monetary contributions from Microsoft Datacenter (Australia) Pty Ltd to Penrith City Council to support delivery of infrastructure including open space and landscaping embellishment within the Mamre Road Precinct, in connection with the future development of a data centre at Lot 2 DP 1271142, 769 Mamre Road, Kemps Creek.

v_incentive_register.granting_body: NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure
v_incentive_register.instrument: NSW Data Centre Guidelines Section 3 service commitments
v_incentive_register.conditions: Available to projects that address the six principles. No fee, no cash, no tax relief. The benefit is departmental labour: a concierge function, pre-assessment support beginning before site selection, SEARs within two months, DA assessment within 75 days, and dedicated post-consent staff.
Whole-of-government coordination across land, energy, water and workforce; not an operator subsidy.

v_incentive_register.instrument: Development Facilitation Program, Part 9A Planning and Environment Act 1987 (Vic)
v_incentive_register.conditions: None. Eligibility is a construction-cost threshold only: above $10m in regional Victoria or $20m in metropolitan Melbourne. There is no performance measure, no efficiency standard, no water standard, no renewable procurement requirement, no community benefit requirement and no local content or training requirement attached to access.

v_influence.instrument: AFR coverage of the Commonwealth grid mandate for data centres
v_influence.position: 'Sounded a note of caution given the global competition to attract investment' in response to the Albanese Government's move to require data centres to generate more power than they use.
v_influence.outcome: The Commonwealth proceeded: on 5 August 2026 the AEMC published advice to the ECMC on mandatory demand offsetting, the Energy Minister lodged rule change requests ERC0448 and ERC0456 on network cost recovery, and NSW introduced the Electricity Infrastructure Investment Amendment Bill 2026.

v_influence.recipient: NSW Legislative Council Public Accountability and Works Committee
v_influence.instrument: Public hearing, Macquarie Room, Parliament House
v_influence.position: Oral evidence in the same session as Endeavour Energy, Ausgrid, the Clean Energy Council, the Business Council's own peer bodies, the UNSW AI Institute, the Australian Information Industry Association, Sydmec and Sweltering Cities.
v_influence.outcome: Recorded in the corrected transcript. In the same hearing a witness stated that cross-subsidisation of industrial use by other customers 'is inconsistent with the framework that we have adopted'.

v_influence.recipient: NSW Legislative Council Public Accountability and Works Committee
v_influence.instrument: Public hearing, Jubilee Room, Parliament House - first witness
v_influence.position: Under parliamentary privilege: data centre operators pay their way; the national electricity rules require all large load users including data centres to pay 100 per cent of connection costs and augmentations; operators will pay $10.3 billion in energy infrastructure to 2030 with $1.1 billion of that excess capacity available for public use; operators 'do not receive subsidies or tax incentives'; ABS water accounts show data centre water use is 0.04 per cent of Australia's and less than 1 per cent of Sydney's; and the widely repeated 25 per cent of Sydney's water by 2035 'is not based in fact' and 'was dismissed by IPART as being unverifiable, and it should be dismissed'. Also that data centres generate 'the highest gross value added per unit of energy of any industrial sector'.
v_influence.outcome: Sydney Water's Managing Director Darren Cleary was asked on 22 May 2026 whether he stood by the 25 per cent forecast and answered 'We do, and we acknowledge the uncertainty'. The IPART characterisation remains unverified - research gap RG-042.

v_influence.recipient: NSW Legislative Council Public Accountability and Works Committee, Inquiry into Data Centres
v_influence.position: Four recommendations: (1) 'Recognise data centres as a strategic economic opportunity for NSW and recalibrate policy settings, regulatory approaches and community narratives to enable and attract investment at scale'; (2) align the NSW approach with the Commonwealth Expectations to create a national and consistent approach so Australia can compete for investment; (3) give the new Investment Delivery Authority the ability to rapidly assess and recommend public infrastructure investments that support major private sector projects; (4) monitor planning reforms to ensure they deliver better performance, 'focusing on efficiency, consistency, and certainty in the planning system'. The submission states that 'the BCA has consistently called for a reduction in regulatory burden, and we do not support introducing additional regulation where it is unnecessary', and cites the BCA's own 2025 Regulation Rumble ranking NSW last for planning system performance as at June 2025.
v_influence.outcome: The NSW Data Centre Guidelines of 17 August 2026 adopted the alignment-with-Commonwealth position (the Guidelines state they are 'consistent with the Australian Government's Expectations ... published in March 2026') and the IDA was already operating, with Round 1 endorsed on 27 March 2026 - five days before this submission was received. Recommendations 3 and 4 concern the IDA and planning performance, both of which remained live policy through 2026. No recommendation sought an environmental, emissions, water, noise, community-benefit, local-content or domestic-compute measure.

v_influence.instrument: Forum membership; co-chair of the Australia India Women's Leadership Forum
v_influence.position: TCS is a member of the government-convened Australia-India CEO Forum and co-chairs its Women's Leadership Forum. The Forum's Director is Jodi McKay, who is concurrently Australia's Senior Trade and Investment Commissioner for South Asia at Austrade (Mumbai) and a former NSW Leader of the Opposition and Cabinet Minister. McKay has posted in that capacity about meeting 'Australia-India CEO Forum member Tata Consultancy Services' and about TCS's Mumbai facility.
v_influence.outcome: Ongoing. A second access channel distinct from the BCA, and one that runs through a serving Commonwealth trade commissioner rather than a domestic peak body.

v_influence.recipient: Public policy debate; cited in Submission No 116
v_influence.instrument: Oxford Economics, 'Surging Data Centre Connection Requests Drive Phantom Demand', 21 November 2025
v_influence.position: That of roughly 44 GW of connection requests linked to data centre proposals received by AEMO in 2025, only about 6 GW of project capacity is expected to proceed and only 2.8 GW of actual electricity draw at maturity - '15 times lower than what is sometimes reported'.
v_influence.outcome: Cited by the BCA to the NSW inquiry and, per the Chair's questioning on 22 May 2026, by Data Centres Australia as well. The NSW Data Centre Guidelines separately cite Oxford Economics work prepared for AEMO estimating that 6 in every 7 MW of connection requests are phantom. The two are consistent: 6 of 7 not proceeding is a 14 per cent conversion rate.

v_influence.recipient: Australian data centre policy debate (position, not advocacy)
v_influence.position: By becoming a hyperscale data centre developer, TCS moved from being a supplier to government into the class of entity whose interests the NSW Data Centre Guidelines, the Commonwealth Expectations and the two parliamentary inquiries are actually about. TPG - its JV partner - is itself a BCA member. TPG's Jim Coulter frames data centers as an asset class at 'the intersection of green energy infrastructure, technology and real estate'.
v_influence.outcome: Announced, subject to conditions precedent and statutory approvals. India-scoped: Chandrasekaran is quoted on building 'GW-scale AI data centers in India'. No Australian HyperVault facility is announced (RG-075).

v_influence.person: Damian Parmenter CBE, former UK Ministry of Defence Director General AUKUS (2023 - 1 Feb 2025); Palantir Technologies UK Ltd 'Senior Counsellor' from July 2025
v_influence.recipient: UK MoD and AUKUS trilateral networks (contacts 'especially in the US and Australia')
v_influence.instrument: ACOBA business appointment advice letter, June 2025 (published c. Sep 2025)
v_influence.position: Senior advisory role providing 'decision support' to the UK Head of Palantir on international defence and security issues, 'focused on international opportunities within Europe and the Indo-Pacific' (Parmenter's own description to ACOBA)
v_influence.outcome: Appointment permitted subject to conditions: no use of privileged information; two-year bars on lobbying the UK government, on using in-office contacts to advantage Palantir (including 'in other governments and organisations'), and on advising on UK government/MoD bids; must not advise on the UK defence sector. Palantir confirmed adherence.

v_influence.instrument: BCA Board appointment, announced jointly with Telstra CEO Vicki Brady
v_influence.position: Access to the governance of Australia's principal general business peak body, whose board carries the CEOs of Telstra, Commonwealth Bank, Wesfarmers, Google Australia and New Zealand and BHP Australia, and the chairman of Gilbert + Tobin. BCA President Geoff Culbert framed the appointment as strengthening the board's 'expertise in innovation and the digital economy'.
v_influence.outcome: Sitting. AirTrunk joined the BCA in or around May 2025, six months before the NSW Data Centre Consultation Paper and eleven months before the NSW Data Centre Guidelines.

v_influence.instrument: BCA Australian AI report, media release 'Business Council unveils Australian AI report to secure leadership by 2028'
v_influence.position: Recommendations include 'Simplify data centre approvals to speed up infrastructure build'.
v_influence.outcome: Published nine months before the NSW Data Centre Consultation Paper (March 2026) and eleven months before the Commonwealth Expectations (23 March 2026).

v_influence.position: That NSW ranked last of the Australian jurisdictions for planning system performance as at June 2025, performing well on transparency but lagging on efficiency, consistency and certainty for proponents.
v_influence.outcome: Cited in Submission No 116 to support Recommendation 4. The ranking is the BCA's own publication, so it is a self-assessed benchmark offered to a parliamentary inquiry as evidence about the state's performance.

v_influence.instrument: BCA membership (member logo published with a 2025/05 asset path)
v_influence.position: Membership of the peak body representing more than 120 chief executives of Australia's largest employers.
v_influence.outcome: Current. Per AFR reporting of 27 November 2025 the BCA counts AirTrunk but not NEXTDC among its members, so the ASX-listed Australian-listed operator is outside the peak body while the Blackstone-controlled one is inside it and on its board.

v_influence.position: Membership of Australia's principal general business peak body - the same body whose board includes AirTrunk founder and CEO Robin Khuda alongside the CEOs of Telstra, Commonwealth Bank, Wesfarmers, Google Australia and New Zealand and BHP Australia, and which made Submission No 116 to the NSW Legislative Council inquiry into data centres on 2 April 2026.
v_influence.outcome: Current as at the April 2025 membership list. Corroborated by a TCS-hosted LinkedIn post stating 'TCS is a member of Business Council of Australia and Australia-India CEO Forum'. The BCA's own /about/ page could not be re-read this session (challenge page, RG-067), so membership is REPORTED from two secondary directions rather than confirmed first-hand. ACCENTURE ALSO APPEARS ON THE SAME LIST, so at least two global systems integrators sit inside the peak body that submitted to the data centre inquiry.

v_influence.person: Mike Kelly, former Labor Minister for Defence Materiel (2013); Australian president of Palantir 2020-2024
v_influence.recipient: Australian defence and national-security procurement networks
v_influence.instrument: ABC Four Corners revolving-door analysis, 23 August 2026
v_influence.position: Australian president of 'the controversial US software and intelligence company Palantir' (ABC's description)
v_influence.outcome: Served 2020-2024. Four Corners counts at least 60 former defence ministers, senior officers and officials now in weapons firms or lobbying companies; AUKUS is described by lobbyist Christopher Pyne as '$368 billion' of lifetime spend and by Senator Shoebridge as 'a multi-billion-dollar feast for lobbyists'.

v_influence.instrument: Political donation disclosure filed on SSD-10330 Roberts Road Data Centre
v_influence.position: A political donation disclosure is filed on the Roberts Road Data Centre project record, whose Schedule 1 applicant is Canberra Data Centres Pty Ltd - a CDC facility, not an AirTrunk one. It is recorded here because it is the only political donation document located anywhere in the 63-project NSW data centre register.
v_influence.outcome: Unread. The document is publicly listed but is a scanned image with no extractable text, so the donor, recipient and amount are unknown.

v_renewable_audit.verification_note: Contradicted on three grounds from the same inquiry record. (1) Sydney Water's Managing Director Darren Cleary was asked directly on 22 May 2026 whether he stood by the 25 per cent forecast and answered 'We do, and we acknowledge the uncertainty', adding that current applications alone represent demand equivalent to a new suburb connecting to the system. The utility that holds the applications stands by the figure. (2) The claim conflates current measured use with a ten-year forward projection: the ABS water accounts describe present consumption, Sydney Water's figure describes demand from applications received. (3) The characterisation of IPART's position as dismissing the figure is unverified and is being checked against IPART's own determination (RG-042). Note also that DCA gave two different figures on two different days - 0.04 per cent of national use and less than 1 per cent of Sydney's on 1 May, and 1.9 per cent as attributed by the Chair on 22 May.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: There is significant misinformation around water use in the public debate. The ABS water accounts show that data centre water use is 0.04 per cent of Australia's water use, and less than 1 per cent of Sydney's water use. The 25 per cent of Sydney's water by 2035 that has been widely repeated in the media and in submissions to this inquiry is not based in fact. It was dismissed by IPART - the independent pricing regulator - as being unverifiable, and it should be dismissed.

v_renewable_audit.instrument_relied_on: on-site solar and long-term PPAs; no certificate type or surrender data specified
v_renewable_audit.lgc_surrender_evidence: Clean Energy Regulator data checked: no data centre operator appears as an LGC-liable entity in the shortfall register (0 of 143 entries, 2001-2025); only two of eight operators reported market-based scope 2 in 2024-25 and none in 2023-24; NEXTDC's market-based figure is 3.6% below its location-based figure; REC Registry holdings are CDC 233,209, Amazon Energy LLC 226,073 and NEXTDC 500, with AirTrunk, Equinix and Global Switch holding none.
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: Contradicted as a sector-wide statement by the primary regulator data. Location-based scope 2 ROSE for every hyperscale operator across 2019-20 to 2024-25: AirTrunk +485% to 553,344 t, Amazon +202% to 405,217 t, CDC +111% to 317,465 t since 2020-21, NEXTDC +64% to 358,353 t. The additionality limb - that operator contracts cause new wind and solar that would otherwise not proceed - is the specific claim Greenpeace Australia Pacific found unproven for every operator analysed in May 2026, and the NSW Government separately records that PPAs to date 'largely skew to solar projects, not the new wind, storage and other firming assets needed for grid stability in NSW'. The 70 per cent figure is not reconcilable with any published dataset: it is not a location-based figure, and the market-based data that could test it is reported by two operators only. Note this is a claim about the whole sector made by a peak body whose board includes an operator whose own 100 per cent claim is separately recorded as CONTRADICTED.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Around 70 per cent of electricity used by data centres is already offset by renewable energy, through a mix of on-site solar generation and long-term renewable power purchase agreements with renewable energy developers to secure electricity supply. Data centre operators committing to long-term contracts 'underpin the financing of new wind and solar capacity that might otherwise struggle to proceed'.

v_renewable_audit.instrument_relied_on: unspecified (generation contracts plus energy attribute certificates)
v_renewable_audit.lgc_surrender_evidence: Clean Energy Regulator corporate NGER data 2019-20 to 2024-25 and market-based scope 2 tables 2023-24 and 2024-25
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: CONTRADICTED as a statement about Australian operations, on primary regulator data. AirTrunk Australia Holding Pty Ltd reported location-based scope 2 of 553,344 t CO2-e in 2024-25, up 485% from 94,528 t in 2019-20; scope 1 rose from 132 t to 4,165 t; net energy consumed rose 625% to 2,886,668 GJ. AirTrunk does not appear in the CER's market-based scope 2 table in either published year, so the 100% renewable claim has no expression in statutory data. AirTrunk holds no account in the REC Registry LGC holdings snapshot (31 July 2026). This does not prove the contractual arrangements do not exist - it proves they are not visible to, or reported through, the regulator, which is precisely the condition the proposed REGO obligation is intended to end.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: AirTrunk states it has signed multiple renewable energy sourcing contracts in Australia and achieved 100% renewable energy by 2025.

v_renewable_audit.site: Cloud Carrier Southern Highlands Data Campus
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: The generation serves new demand rather than displacing coal, so the emissions are additional. Greenpeace estimates ~2.4 Mt CO2-e/yr and notes AEMO's 2026 projections put NSW grid intensity below the level assumed. Also likely to exceed the Safeguard Mechanism facility threshold, unlike grid-powered data centres.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Request for SEARs states the proposed natural gas generation 'is expected to produce lower greenhouse gas emissions than the current coal-dominated grid, resulting in a measurable improvement in overall emissions performance'.

v_renewable_audit.verification_note: Global claim; Australian-specific matching not separately disclosed. The NSW Guidelines note PPAs to date skew to solar rather than the wind, storage and firming assets NSW needs.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Achievement of 100% renewable energy to match energy consumption, and water-positive operations by 2030.

v_renewable_audit.verification_note: The Managing Director stood by the projection under questioning while conceding the ten-year figure could be 20, 10 or 5 per cent, and explained the method: forecasts are based on applications actually received, with obviously duplicative or entirely speculative applications removed. He also gave the committee a reason to trust water applications more than energy applications: by the time a proponent applies for water it has typically already secured its energy connection, so its project is more mature. The no-cross-subsidy commitment is consistent with the IPART water pricing review commissioned on 17 August 2026 and with NSW Guideline Principle 2, but is a statement of intent rather than an enforceable obligation.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Data centre water demand could reach 25 per cent of Greater Sydney demand over ten years; there will not be a cross-subsidy to the consumer, and if a recycled water facility is developed that cost will be borne by the proponents.

v_renewable_audit.instrument_relied_on: National Electricity Rules connection and augmentation cost allocation
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: The 'pay 100 per cent of connection and augmentation costs' limb is corroborated independently: Transgrid's 26 August 2026 position states that where new large users drive network investment beyond their physical connection, costs will be borne by the proponents rather than existing consumers, and the Network Capacity Allocation Policy makes capacity conditional on committing to fund augmentation. The $10.3bn and $1.1bn figures are industry forecasts and are NOT verified. The 'no subsidies or tax incentives' limb is consistent with this database's own finding that no cash concession has been located, but it does not address non-cash state support, which IS documented: the 75-day NSW fast track, Investment Delivery Authority endorsement, a NSW approvals authority for projects above A$1bn, and Victoria's three-month fast track. Given on 1 May 2026, six months before the IDA Round 2 and after Round 1.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Data centre operators pay their way. The national electricity rules require all large load users, including data centres, to pay 100 per cent of connection costs and augmentations to the network. Data centre operators will pay $10.3 billion in energy infrastructure to 2030, and $1.1 billion of that is excess capacity available for public use. Data centre operators do not receive subsidies or tax incentives.

v_renewable_audit.verification_note: This is the second independent industry denial on the record, and it is the closest any primary document comes to answering the NSW inquiry's terms of reference (g)(iii) on 'the extent of public subsidies, concessions or state directed facilitation provided to the sector'. Data Centres Australia made the equivalent claim orally under parliamentary privilege on 1 May 2026 and in its public materials. No revenue-office record either way has been located, which is why RG-007 remains open and why the FOI strategy at reports/RG007_foi_strategy.md is framed to seek policy instruments and aggregate counts rather than named taxpayer assessments. The claim is also narrower than the question asked: it addresses tax concessions and is silent on 'state directed facilitation', which is documented and substantial - the NSW 75-day pathway with a DPHI concierge function and pre-assessment support beginning before site selection, IDA endorsement, and Victoria's Development Facilitation Program. Notably the word 'subsidy' does not appear anywhere in the submission.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Datacentre operators in Australia pay full taxes with no concessions. These companies employ thousands of Australians, pay local taxes and reinvest heavily in new infrastructure.

v_renewable_audit.verification_note: A specific, checkable, operator-level water claim made by a peak body to a parliamentary inquiry, and the most favourable water credential claimed for AirTrunk anywhere in the record. Not verified: the Observatory holds no metered water data for any Australian data centre, Sydney Water supply agreements are not public (RG-017), and NSW planning requirements do not yet specify WUE. If it holds it materially weakens the potable-water critique as applied to AirTrunk, and it would also sit awkwardly with the NEXTDC S7 experience, where recycled water was abandoned because the pipeline planning permission was unavailable - the same infrastructure constraint cannot have bound one operator and not the other without explanation. Highest-value single verification target in the water pillar.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: Recycled water now supplies 55 per cent of AirTrunk's total use, and its Singapore site runs entirely on reclaimed water. (Asserted by the Business Council of Australia in Submission No 116, footnote 23.)

v_renewable_audit.instrument_relied_on: PPAs / vPPAs / green tariffs / RECs plus a small volume of carbon offsets for back-up generators
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: Greenpeace analysis of the EIS: claimed scope 2 emissions fall from 23,574,172 t to 818,316-918,316 t only once procurement strategies are counted, so the entire decarbonisation claim rests on instruments that are not yet contracted or evidenced. Would fail the NSW Guidelines' Principle 3 test (>=40% wind, storage at 25% of generation for 4 hours, 10-year terms, pre-FID additionality).
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: The Mamre Road EIS commits the project to running solely on electricity generated from renewable sources by 2030, with a stated target of 100% renewable electricity procurement through PPAs, virtual PPAs, customer procurement of green tariffs and RECs.

v_renewable_audit.instrument_relied_on: n/a - this is a finding about other parties' claims
v_renewable_audit.lgc_surrender_evidence: Reproduced independently from CER NGER corporate data, market-based scope 2 tables, the LGC shortfall register, the REC Registry holdings snapshot and the Safeguard baselines table.
v_renewable_audit.verification_note: Independently reproduced from primary CER data on 2026-09-18. Of eight data centre operators in the NGER corporate publication, exactly two (NEXTDC and Fujitsu Australia) reported market-based scope 2 in 2024-25 and none did in 2023-24. NEXTDC's market-based figure is only 3.6% below its location-based figure. No operator appears as an LGC-liable entity in the shortfall register (143 entries, 2001-2025). No data centre is a Safeguard Mechanism covered facility (0 of 228). NEXTDC holds 500 LGCs in the REC Registry snapshot; Amazon Energy LLC 226,073; CDC Data Centres Pty Ltd 233,209; AirTrunk, Equinix and Global Switch hold none.
v_renewable_audit.claim_text: No data centre operator analysed in this report adequately proves their claim of driving Australia's renewable energy growth.
